newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-BT, MCI, Telefonica reshape world telecoms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BT, MCI, Telefonica reshape world telecoms.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc and its U.S. partner MCI charged into the vast Spanish-speaking world on Friday, leaving Asia as the only advanced market they have yet to conquer.

In a long-expected move, flagship Spanish telecoms carrier Telefonica de Espana SA jointly announced with BT and MCI on Friday that it had joined BT, allowing BT's Concert alliance with MCI to pursue the booming Latin American communications market which is expected to be worth $60 billion by the year 2000.

The deal, which was unwittingly revealed by Concert's newest partner Portugal Telecom earlier this week, deals a blow to BT and MCI's arch-rival, U.S. phone giant AT&T Corp, and heralds a major change in the telecoms landscape across the Americas and Europe.

"Joining the alliance with Telefonica we will create a telecoms dream team," MCI chairman Bert C Roberts told a joint news conference in Madrid. "We will create the premium telecoms alliance for the next millennium."

The Spanish company said it was also setting up a pan-American joint venture between its international unit and MCI, a move that effectively ends Telefonica's relationship with AT&T and its Unisource European venture.

Telefonica, which partners the national carriers of the Netherlands, Sweden and Switzerland in Unisource, has been dissatisfied with the group, but said the new partnership was compatible with Unisource.

"The alliance with BT and MCI does not harm, according to legal opinions from two international law firms, the deals signed with Unisource," Telefonica chairman Juan Villalonga told Reuters in an interview.
But in the Netherlands, Unisource chairman Lars Berg said the alliance had asked Telefonica to leave.

To reinforce its new deal with Concert, Telefonica is taking a one percent stake in BT and BT is taking a two percent stake in the Spanish group. Each deal is worth about 280 million pounds ($457 million).
Although a joint venture had been expected, the news sent BT shares rising 5.5 pence to 448p, bucking a weaker market trend.
In Madrid, Telefonica shares held steady, and even dipped slightly early on, but shot up 35 pesetas to 3,600 in very heavy volume as Wall Street opened.

The news caps a week of furious negotiations among the new partners who announced that both BT and Telefonica had clinched a strategic alliance with Portugal Telecom which is a key player in South America's biggest market, Brazil.

The Telefonica Internacional SA (TISA) subsidiary will manage a new 50/50 percent held joint venture called Telefonica Panamerica MCI which will dig deeper into the $36 billion South American continent.

TISA already dominates Latin America's communications with an empire spanning Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Peru and Venezuela and is well-placed to take advantage of the continuing privatisation trend in the region.

With a fibre-based network that includes a marine link between Spain and Latin America, the companies plan to establish a state-of-the-art communications portfolio offering voice, data, internet/intranet and video stretching from Alaska to the tip of South America.

In a seemingly inexorable journey across the world, Concert now offers seamless global communications services to customers in 41 countries, focusing on high-margin, multinational corporate customers.
The latest deal with Telefonica means that BT, which entered the Spanish market in 1993, aligns itself with a former rival in a key European market.
Global telecoms groups like Concert are trying to plug holes in their coverage and make up for growth lost in home markets due to increasing competition.

But some experts are also stepping up warnings that vast investments abroad might be too risky. One such investment, which has sparked some concern among the analyst community, is BT's proposed $20 billion merger with MCI.

The planned deal, which won overwhelming shareholder support on Tuesday, is awaiting regulatory clearance in Brussels and the United States. BT expects to win final approval for what will be the largest transatlantic merger in history by the autumn.

"The alliance of BT, MCI and Telefonica will bring us in an extremely strong position in the future with the liberalisation of the telecoms sector in Europe," BT chairman Iain Vallance told the news conference.
BT says it is in constant talks with telecoms operators in the last, major gap in global geographic jigsaw -- the lucrative Asia-Pacific region.
Concert, which needs to service multinational firms with offices in Japan, has been trying to forge a link with Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, the world's biggest telecoms group.

Concert is competing against AT&T-led partnerships such as Unisource and World Partners as well as Global One, an alliance between Deutsche Telekom AG, France Telecom and America's third long-distance carrier, Sprint Corp. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds) ($ = 145.0 Spanish Pesetas)
